findings.claim: Both new dirty-tree guards test the *output* of `git status`, never its exit status. Under `set -euo pipefail`, a command substitution inside `[[ ]]` does not trip `set -e`, so any `git status` failure (index.lock contention from a concurrent git process, a corrupt index, an unreadable submodule) yields empty output and the guard passes as though the tree were clean. The guard therefore fails open on exactly the transient conditions that make a mid-flight branch switch most dangerous, instead of failing closed like its stated intent at line 585.

findings.claim: The ahead notice compares against the remote-tracking ref `origin/main` without any fetch in cmd_apply, and `git rev-list --count origin/main..main` counts only one direction. When main and origin/main have diverged — or when origin/main is simply stale because main was pushed from another machine — the notice still reports `local main is N commit(s) ahead` and recommends `overlay apply --push`, which the remote will reject as non-fast-forward. The advice is actively wrong in the case the notice exists to catch.

findings.claim: The capture guard passes `--untracked-files=no`, so untracked files are exempt — but untracked files survive a branch switch and are exactly what capture is about to write. If a managed file exists untracked on the current branch, `git checkout upstream` at line 598 aborts with "untracked working tree files would be overwritten by checkout", failing after the guard has already declared the tree acceptable. The failure is loud rather than silent, but the guard's error message tells the user to commit or stash *tracked* changes, which does not resolve the untracked case.
